ASEAN not easing Myanmar approach, bloc's special envoy says

ASEAN special envoy and Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro says the grouping is not relaxing its approach to Myanmar under its Five-Point Consensus.

Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa lazaro (centre) delivers her opening statement during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Foreign Ministers’ meeting in Manila on Nov 14, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Pool/Jam Sta Rosa)

MANILA: ASEAN is not relaxing its approach to Myanmar under its Five-Point Consensus, though proposals concerning the country's participation in high-level meetings remain under discussion, the bloc's special envoy on Myanmar said on Saturday (Nov 14). The Five-Point Consensus is ASEAN's main framework for responding to the crisis in Myanmar after a military coup there in 2021. It calls, among other things, for an immediate end to violence and the launch of constructive dialogue among all parties, and offers ASEAN mediation and humanitarian assistance. ASEAN is under increasing pressure ahead of a summit of its leaders in Manila that starts on Sunday to ease a five-year ban on Myanmar's military-backed leaders attending high-level meetings. Thailand and several other members have stepped up engagement with Myanmar despite its ongoing civil war. ASEAN special envoy and Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said a draft review of the Five-Point Consensus was still under negotiation and that "a number of proposals" would be presented to the ASEAN leaders.

"To answer you bluntly, there is no easing (of the approach to Myanmar). There is still the Five-Point Consensus," Lazaro told a press conference, when asked whether the review could lead to adjustments to restrictions on Myanmar's political leadership.

ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus

Following a 2021 military coup , ASEAN has excluded Myanmar from high-level meetings as it has yet to make meaningful progress on the bloc's Five-Point Consensus to end hostilities.  During a meeting in April 2021, all ASEAN leaders reached a consensus about the situation in Myanmar. The five points are: First, there shall be immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and all parties shall exercise utmost restraint. Second, constructive dialogue among all parties concerned shall commence to seek a peaceful solution in the interests of the people. Third, a special envoy of the ASEAN chair shall facilitate mediation of the dialogue process, with the assistance of the secretary-general of ASEAN. Fourth, ASEAN shall provide humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre. Fifth, the special envoy and delegation shall visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned.

Collapse Expand

Asked about Thailand's call to allow Myanmar's foreign minister to participate in meetings of ASEAN foreign ministers, Lazaro said it remained under discussion, but no decision had been made to allow the minister to take Myanmar's seat. "It's still there on the table. It's still a subject of discussion," she said. Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations are set to review their decision to exclude Myanmar when they meet in Manila from Nov 15 to Nov 17.

Microsoft restores service to Outlook and Teams after global outage

The outage crippled online communications for businesses and governments worldwide for over 24 hours.

Microsoft, Teams, Outlook and Copilot logos are seen through broken glass in this illustration taken on Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Dado Ruvic)

Microsoft said on Saturday (Nov 14) that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours. "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company posted on X. Microsoft had said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

It affected government agencies from Singapore , Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.

Related:

'Microsoft-sponsored holiday': Singapore workers scramble to cope with global outage

Singapore government’s Outlook services fully restored after global Microsoft outage

ANOTHER OUTAGE FOR MICROSOFT The outage, reports of which started climbing around 1725 GMT on Thursday, according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online - its cloud-based email and scheduling hub - leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft's workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector's parent company, Ookla. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels. "It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider's email and collaboration tools," said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla. Microsoft shares closed flat at US$523.88 on Friday. The stock has gained roughly 8 per cent so far this year. Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice-president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS. De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between US$300 million and US$500 million, well below the US$400 million to US$1.5 billion financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than 8 million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.

A Microsoft Outlook app icon is seen in this illustration taken on Nov 13, 2026. (Image: Reuters/Dado Ruvic)

Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide. "The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year," said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. "If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider's hands." Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations. TRADES HAD TO BE CONFIRMED BY FAX A spokesperson for the UK government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organisations such as the NHS and London's Metropolitan Police. Lack of access to emails and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police's ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected. The NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records.

Related:

Microsoft 'deeply sorry' as outage triggers global chaos

Faxes, phones and Bluetooth: Microsoft outage forces businesses to find fixes

For businesses, the fallout was widespread. European exchange operator Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates. American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors that were later resolved, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted. The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as cancelling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters. Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said. In the US, electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results on Thursday to Nov 16, while Switzerland's Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday. In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organisations caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyberattack. "The impact that they are dealing with ... is very much on email systems," the minister added.

Source: Reuters/ws

US loses measles-free status after continued spread of the disease: Report

The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades.

The Americas branch of the World Health Organization has reportedly revoked the United States' measles-free status, ending a 26-year run amid continued spread of the disease. (File photo: Reuters/Sebastian Rocandio)

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status, ending a 26-year run after determining the country failed to halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday (Nov 13). The international health body did not immediately respond to a request from Reuters for comment on the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization (WHO) comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades. Some 7,500 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunisation rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines.

United States Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr speaks during an event at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington DC, US, Sep 1, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Evan Vucci)

As part of its evaluation, PAHO reviewed epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to determine whether the same strain of measles had been circulating in the United States uninterrupted for 12 months or longer, a sign of local transmission rather than imported cases. Canada, Spain and the UK recently lost measles-elimination status after review by WHO experts. The US dropped out of WHO but remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch. Dr Erica Schwartz, director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told Reuters in an interview before the decision that if the US lost measles elimination, the agency would be doing "the same exact thing," which entails working with states to encourage immunisation. As of Thursday, 5,182 confirmed cases of measles had been reported in 2026 to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 45 states, New York City and the District of Columbia, surpassing last year's total of 2,289, making it one of the country's worst measles resurgences in decades. "It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles," said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina. Brewer, who chairs an independent advisory panel on measles, presented the CDC's measles status report along with his group's assessment of that information to PAHO on Tuesday.

A measles alert sign hangs outside the entrance to the Cohen Children's Medical Center in New Hyde Park, New York, US, Mar 14, 2025. (Photo: Reuters/Shannon Stapleton)

That report remains confidential, but a source familiar with the CDC's findings said the agency determined the US had 12 months of continuous transmission of the virus. The US achieved its measles-elimination status in 2000. A country can halt transmission when 95 per cent of its population is vaccinated, creating so-called herd immunity that also protects those unable to receive the vaccine. Two doses of the measles vaccine - by far the best way to prevent infection and transmission - provide 97 per cent protection against the virus, which can cause blindness, deafness, brain damage or death. William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said loss of measles elimination was a hit to the United States' reputation as a public health powerhouse. He said it may discourage other countries. For the average American, he added, it means that the United States will continue to have large outbreaks, putting people at risk of disease, hospitalisation and death. To restore measles-elimination status, a country must end transmission and remain free of an outbreak for at least 12 months. The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment.

US flight shutdown exposes deepening air traffic network crisis

The nationwide flight shutdown on Friday (Nov 13) has exposed longstanding weaknesses in the US air traffic control network, raising questions about whether billions of dollars in modernisation efforts can prevent further disruptions.

The Air Traffic Control tower at Chicago O'Hare International Airport, after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop, in Chicago, Illinois, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Jim Vondruska)

FAST

CHICAGO: A communications failure that halted flight departures across the United States on Friday (Nov 13) has renewed scrutiny of the country's ageing air traffic control network, raising questions about its resilience even as the government spends billions of dollars to modernise it. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop , preventing aircraft from departing US airports, following "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers", Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X. Duffy later attributed the outage to a problem with the FAA's legacy network, saying switches and routers had become overloaded with data and went down. It was not immediately clear what caused the equipment overload. The FAA lifted the ground stop after more than four hours, but Duffy warned that it would take time for air traffic operations to return to full capacity.

More than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart US airports on roughly 11,000 flights after 4pm Eastern Time (2100 GMT), shortly after the ground stop began, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Travellers wait in line at ticket counters at LaGuardia Airport in New York after the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide, on Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: AP/Ryan Murphy)

The shutdown came on the same day the White House and Transportation Department sought another US$30.1 billion from Congress to upgrade airports and air traffic control, including US$10.1 billion for air traffic control modernisation. Much of the system's underlying weakness has been documented for years. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2024 that the FAA had classified 51 of its 138 air traffic control systems as unsustainable and another 54 as potentially unsustainable. Together, they accounted for more than three-quarters of the systems reviewed. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters in September that the agency's more than 300 air traffic facilities operated as technological silos, relying in some cases on decades-old computers and telecommunications systems that cannot communicate seamlessly with one another. Some obsolete equipment requires replacement parts obtained through online auction websites or made using 3D printing. BACKUP SYSTEMS UNDER STRAIN An incident in September demonstrated how one communications failure could be compounded by another. After error messages appeared on a telecommunications circuit serving a Philadelphia air traffic control facility, the FAA's contractor switched to a backup fibre-optic line. A construction crew then accidentally severed that line in New Jersey, contributing to widespread disruption. About 9,500 US flights were delayed or cancelled that day. "When it fails, we just don't have the redundancy that we would get if we had a modern architecture," Bedford said at the time. Friday's shutdown was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a failure of the FAA system that distributes critical safety notices to pilots halted departures for less than two hours and disrupted more than 10,000 flights.

A person takes a photo of a screen displaying information on delayed and cancelled flights after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop, at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, Georgia, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Elijah Nouvelage)

Congress approved US$12.5 billion in July 2025 to modernise the country's ageing air traffic control infrastructure, including telecommunications and radar systems. The administration said Friday that 68 per cent of the FAA's legacy copper telecommunications network had been replaced with high-speed fibre. But Bedford warned in September that replacing ageing copper wires with fibre-optic cables alone would not prevent future outages without a modern telecommunications network. The overhaul faces challenges beyond securing money. In September, the Government Accountability Office warned that the FAA lacked a reliable cost estimate and an integrated master schedule for its air traffic control modernisation programme. Instead, as of May, it had 11,389 separate project schedules that were not coordinated, raising the risk of repeated work at the same facilities, delays and cost overruns. The FAA aims to complete the first phase of modernisation by December 2028. But the GAO warned that inadequate planning increased the risk of delays, potentially leaving the agency dependent on outdated systems prone to failure for longer.

US lifts nationwide ground stop, allowing flights to resume after hours of travel chaos

The rare nationwide ground stop order, issued due to a communications problem affecting US air traffic control towers, caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest shutdown since the 9/11 attacks in 2001.

WASHINGTON: The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday (Nov 13) after a communications failure at air traffic control centres caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest nationwide shutdown since the Sep 11, 2001, attacks. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said US airspace reopened at 8.15pm Eastern Time (0115 GMT), but warned that departures would resume gradually and it would take time for airlines to restore normal operations. "It's going to be slow," Duffy told reporters at the White House. More than 6,600 flights were cancelled and 8,600 delayed, with another 1,500 already cancelled for Sunday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said the four-hour nationwide grounding could disrupt airline schedules for days.

Duffy said tens of thousands of passengers were stranded at airports around the country. Three Singapore Airlines (SIA) flights departing the US on Friday were also delayed due to operational issues affecting US airports, the airline said in response to CNA queries. SQ11, operating from Los Angeles to Tokyo-Narita, was delayed for two hours and 30 minutes while SQ25, operating from New York to Frankfurt, was delayed for one hour and 10 minutes. SQ33, operating from San Francisco to Singapore, was also delayed for 43 minutes. The operational issues affecting US airports have been resolved, and there is no impact on other SIA flights, the airline said.  The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by ageing technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

Traffic outside the terminal after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Dulles International Airport, in Dulles, Virginia, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Daniel Heuer

Duane Hanson's "The Traveler" statue rests as people wait in Terminal B during a nationwide ground stop at Orlando International Airport in Orlando City, on Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Getty Images via AFP/Finn Gomez)

Duffy said the trouble began at 3.36 pm when air traffic control centres experienced instability in radar and communications systems. Switches and routers carrying critical data became overloaded, producing inconsistent information and prompting the FAA to halt departures nationwide, he said. "Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data from those routers and because of that we shut the system down," Duffy said, adding at no stage did they completely lose radar or communications and were able to safely land thousands of planes. Duffy said the immediate problem had been fixed and that flying was safe, but warned that a broader overhaul of the ageing air traffic control system was needed to prevent similar failures.

United States Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy takes questions as US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin looks on in the James S Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington DC, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Elizabeth Frantz)

US$50 BILLION AVIATION OVERHAUL Duffy blamed Congress for failing to fund a new system that he said could prevent such outages, and called for US$50 billion to modernise it. Earlier on Friday, before the outage, the White House and Department of Transportation had urged Congress to approve US$30.1 billion to upgrade the nation's ageing airports and air traffic control infrastructure. "What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said. "Give us the money to fix it."

A person waits during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on Nov 13, 2026, in the Queens borough of New York City. (Photo: Getty Images via AFP/Adam Gray)

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was "zero evidence" so far that the outage resulted from a cyberattack or a rogue AI system, although investigators had not ruled out either possibility. "It appears this was mechanically driven, however, we're still looking," Mullin said. The National Security Agency was working with the Department of Homeland Security on the investigation, he added. The outage appeared to be affecting a telecommunications network overseen by L3Harris Technologies, according to two airline officials. The network handles critical radio frequencies used by air traffic controllers to communicate with pilots. L3Harris did not respond to a request for comment. PAIN NOT OVER FOR PASSENGERS Though the ground stop was lifted, the disruption for passengers was far from over. From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded departure halls and airline desks as delays and cancellations mounted and aircraft remained parked at gates.

People wait inside a terminal at Dulles International Airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration issues a national ground stop, in Dulles, Virginia, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Daniel Heuer)

Thousands of passengers faced being stranded overnight. Edward Kargbo, 50, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, had been scheduled to take a 9pm Ethiopian Airlines flight to Lome, Togo. Instead, he planned to spend the night at the airport before a rescheduled flight at 6am on Saturday. “I have to squat the night here,” he said. “I’m stranded.” Louise Maher, 47, was also caught up in the disruption at Newark after her British Airways flight to London was caught up in the aviation meltdown. “I might cry at some point but not yet,” she said. US airlines will not be required to provide compensation to stranded passengers because the carriers were not responsible for the FAA system failures. The only other nationwide ground stop since the Sep 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for about 90 minutes. Investors were already pricing in a financial hit to airlines. Shares of American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines fell between 1 per cent and 2 per cent in after-hours trading, while JetBlue Airways dropped about 3 per cent. American Airlines said it was prioritising flights to smaller cities outside its major hubs and international destinations to position aircraft and crews for a faster recovery.

Commentary: Jensen Huang may prove that the ‘irreplaceable CEO’ is a myth

Jensen Huang's successor will have to figure out how to run a company built around someone who is no longer there, says Beth Kowitt for Bloomberg Opinion.

NEW YORK: “He’s irreplaceable,” Larry Ellison said. The year was 2009 and Oracle’s then-chief executive officer was talking about his friend Steve Jobs, who had recently returned to lead Apple after a liver transplant. Pundits would later go on to say the same about Jeff Bezos, that Amazon.com’s founder and CEO had “no viable successor”. (Both companies, of course, would go on to do just fine without their founders.) It’s worth remembering those prophecies as that word - irreplaceable - gets bandied around with abandon about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down Thursday (Nov 12) after nearly a week of turmoil at the company he cofounded and the industry he anchored.  One of many examples: “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire posted on X, a sentiment Elon Musk endorsed.

Revelations from the New York Times on Wednesday, that Huang had an extramarital relationship with the company’s vice president of healthcare, made it impossible for the board to let him keep his job. While less shocking than Huang’s earlier admission that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, he had clearly violated the company’s code of conduct to “avoid situations where our actions create a conflict”. Before board members could make the case that Huang was the victim of a honeypot scheme. But there’s no convenient explanation for a relationship with a subordinate.

CAN NVIDIA SURVIVE WITHOUT JENSEN HUANG? The board named CFO Collette Kress as the interim CEO, but now its members will have to plan for a future without Huang at the helm. This appears to be something they had rarely considered before, after allowing Huang to structure the company almost entirely around himself. The question now is whether he had also built it to survive without him. As Harvard Business School professor Rakesh Khurana put it to me: “The difference between a cult and a religion is that one outlasts the other.” At Nvidia, the evidence suggests that Huang created a system much more akin to the former.  The company has no chairman, no number two and no public succession plan. Huang had 60 direct reports whose job it was to quickly carry out his decisions, Bloomberg News has reported. Few other executives had a broad purview or responsibilities and instead focused on narrow products or technologies. Other executives had some public exposure but were always overshadowed by Huang, who delivered hours-long keynotes at events.  On earnings calls, as the Wall Street Journal noted, Huang fielded questions from analysts mostly by himself, leaving scripted comments to others - a regular practice at Nvidia but atypical at other companies. His board lacked the expected heavy hitters for a company of its size and import; other than Huang, it has no sitting CEOs.

A REAL FAILURE OF LEADERSHIP? None of that necessarily means Huang can’t be replaced. There was no finding another Jobs or Bezos either - they were both singular leaders. But what they did, which appears to be missing at Nvidia, was methodically build companies designed to carry on their doctrines without them. Both created internal structures that institutionalised their ways of operating and thinking that allowed their successors to thrive: Apple’s stock returned nearly 2,800 per cent during Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure as CEO that ended in September; Andy Jassy has overseen a roughly 50 per cent increase since he took over at Amazon in 2021. At Apple, Jobs was a micromanager who was involved in every detail of the company. But he also taught employees to anticipate how he would solve problems. “The organization has been thoroughly trained to think like Steve,” Fortune reported in 2009. “People could envision, ‘This is what Steve would do.'”  He also had a clear number two in Cook, a manufacturing and supply chain guru, who had a trial run as CEO when Jobs was out on medical leave. Jobs made sure it wasn’t always the Steve Jobs show either. Cook and other executives were given public exposure by appearing alongside him on stage and on earnings calls. (It’s worth noting that Cook is being floated as a possible replacement for Huang, including by President Trump.) At Amazon, Bezos turned his management philosophy into an actionable way of operating - a set of leadership principles that Jassy and other executives helped him write. Bezos picked Jassy as his first shadow, a role in which he followed around the CEO for about 18 months. That’s when the two came up with the idea for Amazon Web Services, and then Bezos gave Jassy a wide berth to run it. By the time Jassy was tapped as CEO, he had already run a hugely important and valuable business. Part of the genius of both Bezos and Jobs was that they figured out how to turn their personal capabilities into corporate culture and competencies.  The parallels are hard to find at Nvidia, which is a real failure of leadership by Huang. His successor will have to figure out how to run a company built around someone who is no longer there. That should be one part of Huang’s legacy that no one tries to replicate.

The incident follows recent security concerns, with US military aircraft moved from British bases reportedly due to threats from Iran.

LONDON: United States Air Force personnel at the RAF Lakenheath base in Britain responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" on Friday (Nov 13) evening, although no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a US Air Force spokesperson said. "We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families," the spokesperson added. Britain's Ministry of Defence said US Air Force Security Forces personnel had responded to reports of unauthorised drone activity and that the situation had been resolved. "We are working closely with them to establish the facts. We will provide updates in due course," a ministry spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

T he US has in recent weeks moved bombers that had been used to strike Iran out of Britain, and relocated huge refuelling aircraft from Britain to Germany. The Wall Street Journal has reported that the refuelling aircraft were moved due to a threat from Iran. The bombers left RAF Fairford on security grounds after a group of men approached the base in white vans in the middle of the night on Sep 27. Two men were charged last month in relation to that incident, with prosecutors alleging one of them had tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain. The US Justice Department said this week that a member of an Iran-backed militia had plotted to attack the Fairford air base while detained in the US on criminal charges. Britain's domestic spy chief said in October that Iran had stepped up attempts to hit harder targets such as military sites in Britain. Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of malign activity in Britain, where the authorities have for a number of years accused it of being involved in plots and attempted assassinations against dissidents and Israeli and Jewish targets. Germany has blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August after airport workers found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, an important civilian freight and NATO logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for several giant Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.
